Fiscal Recovery Funds in America's Metropolitan Cities

How much 770 U.S. metropolitan cities received from the American Rescue Plan's State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds, how fast they spent it, what they spent it on, and how crime moved, based on the project reports cities filed with the U.S. Treasury through March 2025.

        Circles are sized by total award. Drag to pan, use the buttons to zoom, and select a circle to see that city.
        Coverage. The 770 incorporated places with more than 50,000 residents (American Community Survey 2015 to 2019) that received a direct SLFRF award as metropolitan cities, including consolidated city-county governments such as New York, Philadelphia, Nashville, and Louisville, and excluding Washington, DC and Puerto Rico.
        Sources. Allocations and project data: U.S. Department of the Treasury, SLFRF Project and Expenditure Report public data, quarterly releases with data through December 2021 and June 2022 to March 2025 (the March 2022 release did not include these cities). Budgets and categories come from the release with data through December 2024, the last one to report adopted budgets; where a project reported no adopted budget, its obligations are shown and marked. City budgets: U.S. Census Bureau, 2017 Census of Governments, general expenditure excluding utilities and city-owned hospitals. Population: American Community Survey 2015 to 2019. Crime: homicide, violent crime, and property crime from the Real-Time Crime Index (AH Datalytics), monthly counts summed over the trailing twelve months, for the cities and measures it covers. Its counts follow each agency's own published data, so levels can differ from FBI figures, while trends within a city are comparable. For other cities and measures, the FBI Uniform Crime Reports offenses known files (Kaplan, 2025), calendar-year counts from police agencies reporting all twelve months, with partial-year records and clear reporting breaks dropped. Rates are per 100,000 residents of 2019.
        Reading the numbers. Spending is what cities reported as cumulative expenditures. "Revenue replacement" is money cities could use for general government services, so its project descriptions are often brief.
